"AI was supposed to have done XYZ"???? The pace of AI progress hasn't been fast enough? Are you even speaking seriously? It's hard to take this video seriously with that title. Right off the hop. Anyone citing history as a guide for how obsolescence via AI will progress, is completely misunderstanding the world they live in. AI has no analogue in history. Your assertion is dead in the water from the outset. At best you are reaching for misrepresentative analogies, which do not reflect the scale nor the capabilities emerging from AI at an exponential pace. You aren't recognizing scale first of all (AI can replace 10000 CSRs almost as easily as 1). So citing increased demand is nonsense. Double it. Quintiple it. 100x. AI is still replacing that job. Once it can replace 1, it can replace 1000s or "all". And the number of human overseers decreases all along the way. Demand IS increasing almost invisibly, because it's not producing jobs (for example, people use AI therapy daily, but it's not even materializing as new therapist jobs - the increased demand is being swallowed invisibly and isn't even showing up on economic reports). #2 your data is old. AI is already replacing workers, from programmers (originally argued as the most immune lol) to CSRs, to professionals, in companies all over the map. #3 you aren't recognizing the pace. AI was showing us videos 5 years ago of people with six fingers and 3 elbows. Now it's fooling some people, scamming the elderly, and occasionally leading even savvy viewers to question if a human being is AI. The pace is unlike any other obsolescence in history. The final barrier was supposed to be manual skills and labor. But today we are finding that AI control is accelerating the capabilities of robots. It took 20 years to bring robots to the point of walking in a jerky fashion. Now AI has taken over, and within the space of 5 years robots are doing jumping spin-kicks, and run faster than Usain Bolt (literally). It won't be long as long as we thought before they are managing farm equipment. I think the biggest discrepancy is viewing AI as a tool. This is false. AI is not a tool. AI is the tool AND the labor. Therefore, increased demand is swallowed instantly and nearly invisibly by simply creating more instances of that labor. AI can help a worker do their job not in the sense of making them more efficient, but in the sense that they are no longer doing anything. And shifting human workers to oversight roles is rapidly becoming less necessary, as AI is approaching (and will soon surpass) the reliability of the human overseers.

Just my two cents, you can never predict the job market. Consequently, I've encountered people with "A.I." component degrees that wind up employed. It isn't as black and white as you make it out to be. This is coming from someone majoring in Biotechnology.

I agree to the extent that most of these examples were very specialized where AI takes already existing tasks and improves them, sometimes massively. But the real AI threat is the generalist systems, the ones that are ill-defined, hunting for a market that will eventually be profitable.
An ornithologist makes $63K a year. (Scientist of Birds)

Will AI take my job? Probably not. Will it result in me getting paid significantly less? Probably. AI has massively shrunk the skill gap that used to exist between a fresh out of college hire and a 10-20 year software industry veteran.

I'm glad that you apologised for the harsh language at the end of the main part of your video. You made good points throughout. I'm on board with the idea of AI automating more of the tasks of people's jobs and ushering in a new age of prosperity. But you completely ignored the very real human and environmental cost of AI infrastructure.
